en: The Paiṅgala Upaniṣad
A General Upaniṣad Belonging to the Śukla Yajurveda.
I meditate upon Rāma everywhere— the one known through the Paiṅgala Upaniṣad, whose form is supreme bliss, and who is the majesty of the supreme syllable.
Oṃ. That is full, this is full; from the full, the full arises.
When the full is taken from the full, only the full remains.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.

Then Paiṅgala, having approached Yājñavalkya after twelve years of service, asked: "Please teach me the supreme secret of Kaivalya. Yājñavalkya said: "O Somya, in the beginning this was Being alone. That is Brahman—eternal, liberated, changeless, truth, knowledge, bliss, perfectly full, ancient, one without a second."

In that [state], just as there is water, silver, a man, or lines upon a desert mirage, a mother-of-pearl shell, a post, or crystal, there existed the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), composed of the qualities of red, white, and black, which is indefinable due to the equilibrium of the *guṇas*. That which was reflected therein was the consciousness of the Witness (*sākṣicaitanya*). Then, having undergone modification, it became the power of concealment called the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), in which *sattva* predominates; that which was reflected therein was the consciousness of the Lord (*īśvaracaitanya*).

He, whose *māyā* is under his own control, is omniscient and the primordial creator of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the universe]; he exists in the form of the sprout of the world. He manifests the entire universe, which was previously dissolved within himself. By the power of the karma of living beings, he spreads it out like a cloth; and upon the exhaustion of the karma of living beings, he again causes it to disappear. Within him alone, the entire universe exists like a folded cloth. From the power of concealment presided over by the Lord, there arose the power of projection called *mahat*, in which the quality of *rajas* predominates.

That which was reflected therein was the consciousness of Hiraṇyagarbha. He is the presiding deity of the principle of *mahat* (the Great One), possessing a body that is both distinct and indistinct. From the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*) presided over by Hiraṇyagarbha, there arose a gross power called the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) in which the quality of *tamas* predominates. That which was reflected therein was the consciousness of Virāṭ. He is the presiding deity of that [power], possessing a distinct body; he is Viṣṇu, the protector of all gross things, the primary Puruṣa. From that Self, space (*ākāśa*) was produced; from space, air (*vāyu*).

From wind comes fire; from fire, water; from water, earth. These five subtle elements (tanmātras) consist of the three qualities (guṇas). Desiring to create the world, the Source of the universe, presiding over the quality of darkness (tamas), desired to make those subtle elements into gross material beings.

Having divided each of the limited elements of creation into two parts, and then having divided them again into four, He combined them into five by means of their respective second portions; with these quintuplicated elements (*pañcīkṛta-bhūta*), He created infinite millions of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) along with the gross bodies (*sthūla-śarīra*) situated within the spheres appropriate to each egg. Having divided the *rajas* portions of the five elements into four parts, He created the vital breath (*prāṇa*) consisting of five functions from three of those parts. With the fourth part of those [elements], He created the organs of action (*karmendriya*).

Having divided the *sattva* portion of those [elements] into four parts, he created the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) consisting of the fivefold functional activity from the combination of three parts. From the fourth part of the *sattva* of those [elements], he created the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriyāṇi*). From the totality of the *sattva*, he created the guardians of the organs. Having been created, these were cast into the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*). By his command, they remained pervading the collective egg. By his command, Virāṭ, endowed with ego (*ahaṅkāra*), protected the gross bodies.

By His command, Hiraṇyagarbha protected those subtle elements situated within the cosmic egg; without Him, they were unable to vibrate or exert themselves. Desiring to endow them with consciousness, Brahmā pierced the apertures of the cosmic egg and the heads of all individual beings and entered therein. Then, although they were insentient, they performed their respective functions as if possessed of consciousness. The omniscient Lord, accompanied by a trace of *māyā*, entered an individual body and, deluded by it, assumed the state of a *jīva*.

Due to its identity with the three bodies (*śarīra-traya*), it attains the state of being an agent and an enjoyer. Endowed with the conditions of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, fainting, and death, it becomes agitated like a water-wheel; born and dying, it revolves according to the analogy of a potter’s wheel. Thus ends the first chapter. 1.1.103.

Then Paiṅgala said to Yājñavalkya: "How did the Lord (Īśa), the all-pervading creator, sustainer, and destroyer of all worlds, come to possess the state of a living being (jīvatva)? Yājñavalkya replied: "I shall explain the nature of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (Īśvara) after first analyzing the emergence of the gross, subtle, and causal bodies; listen with attention and one-pointedness. The Lord, having taken minute portions of the five gross elements that have been quintuplicated (pañcīkṛta), created the gross bodies consisting of both the individual (vyaṣṭi) and the collective (samaṣṭi) in their proper order."

The skull, skin, intestines, bones, flesh, and nails are portions of earth; blood, urine, saliva, sweat, and so forth are portions of water; hunger, thirst, heat, delusion, sexual desire, and so forth are portions of fire; movement, lifting, respiration, and so forth are portions of air; and desire, anger, and so forth are portions of space. The aggregate of these, accumulated through karma, endowed with skin and other coverings, the locus of the conceit of states such as childhood and the like, and the substratum of many defects, becomes the gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*).

Then, from the aggregate of three parts of the rajasic portion of the unquintuplicated (*apañcīkṛta*) great elements, he created the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The functions (*vṛtti*) of the vital breath are prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna. The secondary vital breaths (*upaprāṇa*) are nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. Their locations are the heart, anus, navel, throat, and all the limbs. From the fourth part of the rajasic quality of the elements beginning with space (*ākāśa*), he created the organs of action (*karmendriya*). Speech, hands, feet, anus, and the generative organ are their [the organs'] functions; speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and sexual pleasure are their respective objects.

Thus, from the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the three parts of the *sattva* constituent of the elements, he created the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). The internal organ consists of mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), thought (*citta*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*); their functions (*vṛtti*) are volition (*saṅkalpa*), determination (*niścaya*), memory (*smaraṇa*), and self-identification (*abhimāna*), and these are their respective objects. Their locations are the throat, the mouth, the navel, the heart, and the space between the eyebrows. From the fourth part of the *sattva* constituent of the elements, he created the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*). The ears, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose are their functions; sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their objects.

The guardians of the causes are the Lord of the Quarters (Dik), Vāyu, Arka (the Sun), Pracetas, the two Aśvins, Vahni (Fire), Indra, Upendra (Viṣṇu), Mṛtyu (Death), Candra (the Moon), Viṣṇu, the Four-faced One (Brahmā), and Śambhu. Now, there are five sheaths (*kośas*): those consisting of food (*annamaya*), vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), mind (*manomaya*), consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), and bliss (*ānandamaya*). That which, having come into being through the essence of food and having attained growth through the essence of food, dissolves into the earth—which itself consists of the essence of food—is the sheath consisting of food. That is the gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*). The fivefold vital breaths, beginning with *prāṇa*, together with the organs of action (*karmendriyas*), constitute the sheath consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya-kośa*).

The intellect (*buddhi*) together with the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) is the sheath consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamayakośa*). These three sheaths constitute the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*). Ignorance regarding one's true nature (*svarūpājñāna*) is the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamayakośa*); it is the causal body (*kāraṇaśarīra*). Now, the pentad of the organs of knowledge, the pentad of the organs of action (*karmendriya*), the pentad beginning with breath (*prāṇa*), the pentad beginning with space (*viyat*), the fourfold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and desire, action, and darkness—these are the eight cities. By the command of Īśa, having entered the individual body (*vyaṣṭideha*) of Virāj and presiding over the intellect, [the Self] attained the state of being the universe (*viśvatva*).

The *vijñānātman*, the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), known as *viśva*, is the empirical self who identifies with the gross body during the waking state; it is called *viśva* because it is the locus of manifold activity (*karma-bhūri*). By the command of the Lord (*Īśa*), the *sūtrātman* enters the individual subtle body (*vyaṣṭi-sūkṣma-śarīra*) and, presiding over the mind (*manas*), attains the state of *taijasa*. It is called *taijasa* because it is phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*) and fashioned in the dream state. By the command of the Lord, the one whose limiting adjunct is *māyā* (*māyopādhi*), conjoined with the unmanifest (*avyakta*), enters the individual causal body (*vyaṣṭi-kāraṇa-śarīra*) and attains the state of *prājña*.

The one who is disconnected [from objects] and possesses ultimate reality, characterized by the conceit of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), is called *prājña*. For the *jīva* whose ultimate nature is veiled by the ignorance of a subtle trace of the unmanifest (*avyakta-leśa*), statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) proclaim its identity with Brahman; this does not apply to the other two states, the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) and the illusory (*prātibhāsika*). That very consciousness which is reflected in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the one that undergoes the three states.

Having reached the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, it becomes agitated like a water-wheel, remaining as if born and as if dead. Now, there are five states: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, swoon, and death. The state of waking occurs when there is the cognition of grasping objects such as sound through the sense organs of knowledge, such as the ears, which are possessed by their respective presiding deities. In that state, the individual soul (jīva), having reached the space between the eyebrows and pervading from head to foot, becomes the performer of all activities such as seeing, hearing, and so forth.

And he becomes the enjoyer of various fruits; having gone to another world, he alone enjoys the fruit acquired through his karma. Tired from worldly activities like a sovereign emperor, he stands taking recourse to the path in order to enter the inner palace. When the instruments [of perception] cease, the state of dreaming occurs, wherein there is a manifestation in the form of the grasped and the grasper, arising from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the waking state, like a waking up.

In that state, Viśva itself, due to the cessation of waking-world activity, moves into the midst of the *nāḍīs* and, attaining the state of Taijasa, illuminates the manifold variety of the world in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) by its own light and experiences it according to its desire. The state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) has the mind alone as its instrument. Just as a bird, exhausted from flying, folds its wings and proceeds toward its nest, so too the individual soul (*jīva*), having functioned within the phenomenal world of waking and dreaming, becomes weary and, entering into ignorance (*ajñāna*), enjoys its own bliss.

Suddenly, as if struck by a hammer or a staff, a state resembling death occurs—a fainting fit (*mūrchā*)—wherein one trembles due to the sensory aggregates (*indriyasaṅghāta*) being overwhelmed by fear and ignorance. Distinct from the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and fainting, there is the state of death, which bestows fear upon all living beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, and results in the casting off of the gross body (*sthūladeha*).

Having withdrawn the organs of action, the organs of knowledge, their respective objects, and the vital breaths, the individual soul (jīva)—accompanied by desire and karma, and enveloped by the veil of ignorance—attains another body and goes to another world. Due to the ripening of the fruits of past actions, it finds no rest, like a worm caught in the eddy of a whirlpool. Through the full maturation of virtuous deeds, the desire for liberation arises in men at the end of many births. Then, by taking refuge in a true guru and serving him for a long time, someone attains liberation from bondage.

Bondage is caused by a lack of inquiry; liberation arises from inquiry. Therefore, one should always inquire. It is possible to ascertain the true nature [of reality] through superimposition and negation (*adhyāropa-apavāda*). Therefore, one should always inquire: when the states of being a living soul (*jīva*) and the state of the world are sublated, Brahman alone remains as non-different from the inner self (*pratyag-abhinna*). Thus ends the second chapter. 2.

Then Paiṅgala questioned Yājñavalkya, saying, "Explain the exposition of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya). Yājñavalkya replied: "One should perform the contemplation [as follows]: 'That art thou'; 'Thou art That'; 'Thou art Brahman'; 'I am Brahman. In this context, that which is characterized by mediacy and manifoldness, possessing attributes such as omniscience and having Māyā as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), which is the source of the universe and characterized by Being-Consciousness-Bliss, is denoted by the word 'That' (tat-pada-vācya)."

That very consciousness, when conjoined with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and serving as the objective support for the notion of "I" (*asmat-pratyaya*), becomes the denotable meaning (*vācya*) of the term *tvam*. Setting aside the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the Supreme and the individual soul—namely, *māyā* and *avidyā*—the Brahman that is non-different from the inner self (*pratyag-abhinna*) is the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) of the terms *tat* and *tvam*. The investigation into the meaning of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*), such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) or "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), constitutes *śravaṇa*. The one-pointed reflection upon the meaning of what has been heard constitutes *manana*.

When the object of inquiry has been rendered free from doubt through hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), the steady fixing of the mind upon that reality with one-pointedness constitutes *nididhyāsana*. Abandoning both the meditator and the act of meditation, the mind—like a lamp placed in a windless spot—becomes focused solely on the object of meditation; this is *samādhi*. At that time, the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) directed toward the Self arise without being perceived. These are inferred from memory. By this very process, the millions of karmas accumulated throughout this beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) reach their dissolution.

Then, through proficiency in practice, a thousandfold streams of nectar rain down perpetually. Thereupon, those most skilled in yoga call this the "Cloud of Dharma" (dharmamegha) samādhi. When the web of latent impressions (vāsanā) has been entirely dissolved by this means, and when the accumulation of karma—both merit and demerit—has been uprooted from its very foundation, even that which was previously beyond perception arises as an unimpeded, direct realization, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand. At that time, one becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta). The Lord [desiring] to perform the de-pentadification (apañcīkaraṇa) of the pentadified elements (pañcīkṛtabhūta), He willed thus.

Having reduced the cosmic egg and the worlds contained within it—which exist in the form of effects—to their causal state, one then unifies the subtle body, the organs of action, the vital breaths, the organs of knowledge, and the fourfold internal organ; having joined all elemental things into their cause, the five gross elements, earth dissolves into water, water into fire, fire into air, air into ether, ether into the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*), the ego-principle into the Great Principle (*mahat*), the Great Principle into the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the Unmanifest is gradually dissolved into the Puruṣa.

Virāṭ, Hiranyagarbha, and Īśvara dissolve into the Supreme Self upon the dissolution of their respective adjuncts (*upādhi*). The gross body, which is accumulated through karma arising from the fivefold-combined (*pañcīkṛta*) great elements, attains the state of non-fivefold-combination (*apañcīkaraṇa*) through the exhaustion of karma and the ripening of virtuous deeds; having become unified with the subtle body and attained the state of being a causal form, that cause dissolves into the immutable inner Self (*pratyagātman*). Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña dissolve into the inner Self through the dissolution of their own respective adjuncts.

The egg [of the universe], burnt by the fire of knowledge, becomes dissolved along with its causes into the Supreme Self. Thereafter, the Brahmin, having become composed, should always effect the identity of the words "That" and "Thou. Then, like the sun when the clouds have cleared, the Self manifests. Having meditated upon the Self situated within like a lamp inside a jar—one who is the size of a thumb, consisting of smokeless light—he should meditate on that immutable, unchanging Being who shines within.

That sage who remains in meditation from the time he is not asleep until his death should be known as one liberated while living (jīvanmukta); he is blessed and has accomplished his purpose. Having abandoned the state of being liberated while living when his own body is surrendered to time, he enters the state of disembodied liberation (videhamukti), just as the wind enters a state of motionlessness.
That which is without sound, without touch, without form, imperishable, likewise without taste, eternal, and without smell;
beginningless and endless, beyond the Great (Mahat), and constant.
That very [reality] remains stainless and free from affliction. Thus [it is said]. (3.4)
Thus ends the third chapter. || 3 ||

Then Paiṅgala questioned Yājñavalkya: "What is the action of the man of knowledge, and what is his state? Yājñavalkya replied: "The seeker of liberation, endowed with humility and other virtues, delivers twenty-one generations of his lineage. By the mere fact of knowing Brahman, he delivers one hundred and one generations of his lineage. Know the Self to be the rider in the chariot, and the body to be the chariot itself. Know the intellect to be the charioteer, and the mind to be the reins. (4.1)

The wise say that the senses are the horses and the sense-objects are their paths; they say the hearts are the moving celestial chariots. (4.2) The great seers say that the Self, when joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer; therefore, Nārāyaṇa himself is well-established within the heart. (4.3) Until the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma, he conducts himself like a snake shedding its skin; like the moon, the embodied soul moves about—liberated and homeless. (4.4) Whether at a sacred ford or in the house of an outcaste, having cast off the body, he attains absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).

Having cast off the vital breaths, he attains absolute liberation (*kaivalya*). After that, one should offer him the *digbali* oblation, or else perform the rite of digging [the earth]. The renunciation of a man has been prescribed; it is never for anyone else. (4.5) There is no impurity, no fire-ritual, no funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), and no water-libation for a mendicant who has become one with Brahman. One should not perform the *pārvaṇa* and other such rites for him. (4.6) Just as there is no burning of what is already burnt, nor cooking of what is already cooked, so too for one whose body has been consumed by the fire of knowledge, there is neither *śrāddha* nor [other] ritual action. (4.7)

One should serve the guru until the very end of one's physical existence. One should behave toward the wife and the sons of the guru as one does toward the guru himself. (4.8) With a pure mind, being of the nature of pure consciousness, patient—one who thinks, "I am that patient one"—when, through the attainment of knowledge (*jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*), the Knowable Supreme Self is established in the heart and the body has reached the state of attained peace, then [the world] becomes empty of light, mind, and intellect. What need is there for water for one who is satiated by nectar?

Having thus known one's own Self, what further need is there for the Vedas? For the yogi satisfied by the nectar of knowledge, there is nothing left to be done; if there were anything remaining, he would not be a knower of reality. Though situated far away, the inner Self is not distant; though residing within the physical body, it is all-pervading. Having made the heart pure and having contemplated that which is free from affliction, one should perceive the supreme bliss, seeing: "I alone am everything, the Supreme. (4.9)

Just as water poured into water, milk into milk, or ghee into ghee becomes indistinguishable, O Thunderbolt-wielder, so it is with the individual self and the supreme self. (4.10) When the body is illumined by knowledge and the intellect takes on the form of the indivisible whole, then the wise man shall burn away the bondage of karma with the fire of the knowledge of Brahman. Thereafter, he abides in the pure, supreme Lord known as non-duality, resembling the stainless sky; like water that has entered into water, he remains established in his own essential nature, free from all limiting adjuncts. (4.11)

The self, with its subtle body like space, is not seen; the inner self is like the wind. That inner self, whose nature is motionless both externally and internally, perceives through the torch of knowledge. (4.12) Wherever the knower dies, and by whatever means of death, he attains dissolution there, just as the all-pervading sky [dissolves] into itself. (4.13) He truly understands the self’s dissolution to be like that of the space within a jar; he goes toward the supportless light of knowledge everywhere. (4.14)

A man standing on one foot for thousands of years does not equal even a sixteenth part of this yoga of meditation (dhyāna-yoga). (4.15) One may desire to know all this—that which is knowledge and that which is to be known—even with a lifespan of a thousand years, yet one does not reach the end of the scriptures. (4.16) The object to be known is merely the imperishable essence (akṣara-tanmātra), and life itself is fickle; therefore, casting aside the web of scriptures, one should worship that which is Truth. (4.17) Infinite is ritual action, as are purity, recitation (japa), and likewise sacrifice.

One undertakes pilgrimages to sacred fords only so long as one does not find the ultimate reality. "I am Brahman"—this constant realization is the cause of liberation for the great-souled ones. There are two words for bondage and liberation: "mine" and "not mine. A living being is bound by the thought "mine," and is liberated by the thought "not mine. Indeed, when the mind reaches the state beyond the mind (*unmanī*), duality is no longer perceived. When the state beyond the mind is attained, that is the supreme state. Wherever the mind goes, there is the supreme state.

4.21–22 || There, everywhere, the Supreme Brahman is equally established. One might strike at empty space with one's fists; one afflicted by hunger might try to crack open a grain husk. He who does not know "I am Brahman"—for him, liberation does not arise. He who constantly studies this Upaniṣad becomes purified by fire; he becomes purified by wind; he becomes purified by the sun; he becomes purified by Brahman; he becomes purified by Viṣṇu; he becomes purified by Rudra.

He becomes as one who has bathed in all sacred fords; he becomes as one who has studied all the Vedas; he becomes as one who has performed the observances of all Vedic vows. By him, the fruits of reciting a hundred thousand *rudra* hymns from the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* are obtained. Ten thousand *praṇavas* have been recited by him. He purifies ten ancestors and ten descendants. He becomes a sanctifier of the company at a meal. He becomes great.

One becomes purified from the sins of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold, violating the teacher’s bed, and associating with those who commit such acts. The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye stretched across the sky. The inspired poets, ever vigilant, kindle that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Om. Truth. Thus ends the Upanishad. Om. All is full. Thus the peace invocation.
Thus ends the Paiṅgala Upaniṣad.
